concept.name: Stablecoin supply
concept.definition: Stablecoin supply is the total outstanding issuance of stablecoins — cryptocurrencies designed to hold a stable value against a reference asset, usually the US dollar — and is tracked as a proxy for dry powder and fiat liquidity in the crypto economy.
concept.intuition: It is the pile of dollar chips sitting at the crypto casino's tables: when it grows, new fiat-backed buying power is entering; when it shrinks, capital is cashing out.
concept.mechanics: Stablecoins preserve their peg by design: asset-linked issuers (USDT, USDC) back tokens with reserves and mint/redeem against fiat, while crypto-collateralized designs (Dai) mint against overcollateralized vaults and algorithmic ones adjust supply programmatically. Aggregate supply across issuers and chains is observable on-chain and, per FSB/BIS definitions, reflects how much of the ecosystem's settlement happens in dollar terms.
concept.failure_modes: Reserve opacity or a run on an issuer can break the peg (redemptions forcing fire sales of reserve assets); bridge fragmentation splits supply across chains where a wrapped version is only as good as its bridge; regulatory action against a major issuer is systemic for the whole market.
concept.misconceptions: Stablecoin supply growth is not pure bullish flow — some of it rotates from existing crypto sales into stables (risk-off) rather than fresh fiat in. 'Backed 1:1' claims have historically been revised (Tether's composition disclosures), so attestations, not labels, are the evidence.
concept.example: Total stablecoin market value grew from ~$14B in August 2020 to over $300B by 2026, with USDT (~$186B) and USDC (~$79B) comprising roughly 85% of circulation — a scale the BIS flags as a financial-stability consideration.

citations.source: Arner, Auer & Frost, BIS Working Paper No 905: Stablecoins - risks, potential and regulation
